segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Hello, this is 6 Minute English from BBC Learning English. I'm Phil.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: And I'm Georgie.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: In the words of a famous 1960s pop song, breaking up is hard to do.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Divorce, when a married couple who no longer want to be together separate,

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: can be one of life's toughest experiences.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: During the 1990s, divorce rates in Europe and America were the highest in the world,

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: with almost half of all marriages ending in divorce.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: But since then, the trend has reversed and divorce rates in the West have slowed.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Meanwhile, however, the number of couples divorcing in other parts of the world is on the rise.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: In this programme, we'll be hearing how divorce is talked about in different countries

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: and, as usual, we'll be learning some useful new vocabulary.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: But first, I have a question for you, Georgie.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: In Britain, one day of the year in particular is known by divorce lawyers and relationship counsellors as Divorce Day.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: But which day is it?

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: A. Christmas Day.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: B. The first Monday of the new year.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Or C. Midsummer's Day, the 24th of June.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: I think Divorce Day is the first Monday of the year.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: OK Georgie, we'll find out if that's the correct answer later in the programme.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Getting married very young and differences between partners backgrounds or interests are two common causes for couples to grow apart Today Marina Adshade is a professor at the University of British Columbia

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: who studies the economics of sex and relationships.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: But her life has a very different beginning,

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: as she told BBC World Service programme The Global Story.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: I married really young. I had no education.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: I married somebody who was older than me, who had a lot of education, and our relationship worked well for a while.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: And then in my late 20s, I decided to go back to school.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: I no longer wanted to be a stay-at-home mother, which was what I was doing in my 20s.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: And that change in our situation for us just became completely unresolvable.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: And I think this is true for a lot of marriages because people's situation changes over their lives.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Maybe they want children and maybe they change their minds.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Marina started her married life as a stay-at-home mum,

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: a woman who stays home to take care of the children and manage the household.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Marina married an older man, and although their relationship started well,

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: over time they developed different ideas about what they wanted from life.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Marina and her husband changed their minds.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: They changed an earlier decision they had made.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Growing apart is one of the most frequently given reasons for divorce,

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: And eventually, Marina and her husband's problems became unresolvable, not able to be fixed or satisfactorily ended.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Marina experience is typical of someone who finds themselves trapped in a marriage that no longer works Yet unfortunately due to economic or emotional reasons many people stay trapped

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: So what can be done?

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Now, some countries are looking to the authorities rather than the couple themselves for a solution.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Here, Lucy Hockings, presenter of BBC World Service's The Global Story,

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: and divorce councillor Joanna Gosling discuss a new strategy being used in China.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: There was an interesting thing they did in China where they introduced this cooling off period.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: So the government enforced this.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Does that work when the government intervenes in a situation like this

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: and makes people behave or do things in a certain way?

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: If nothing changes in the dynamic between two people,

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: being told that they've got to cool off and wait a bit longer,

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: I don't think is going to make them suddenly realise that they want to be together.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: It might be an idea for states to invest in communication programmes for these couples

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: because that's invariably why relationships fall apart.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: In response to rising divorce rates, in 2021,

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: the Chinese government introduced a 30-day cooling-off period for couples wanting to separate.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: A cooling-off period is a period of time in which two groups who are arguing

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: can try to improve the situation before taking further action.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: However, it's unusual for governments to intervene, to become involved, in people's private lives this way.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Joanna doubts a cooling period will work especially as the main reason for relationships failing is non She says a lack of communication is invariably well always the reason for divorce

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: On the plus side, by communicating openly,

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: maybe with the professional help of a relationship counsellor,

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: saving a marriage is possible.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: I think it's time you reveal the answer to your question, Phil.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: You asked about divorce day in Britain,

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: and I guessed it was the first Monday of the new year.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Good guess, Georgie, because that's the correct answer.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Divorce day is the first Monday of the year.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: OK, let's recap the vocabulary we've learnt in this programme,

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: starting with stay-at-home mum,

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: a phrase for a woman who stays home to care for her children and manage the household.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: If you change your mind, you change an earlier decision you made or opinion you had.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: If a problem is unresolvable, it cannot be satisfactorily solved or fixed.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: A cooling-off period is a period of time for two people to try to resolve their differences.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: It can also mean an agreed length of time in which someone can change their mind about something they've agreed to buy.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: To intervene means to become involved in a difficult situation in order to improve it.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: And finally, the adverb invariably means always.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Once again, our six minutes are up, but remember to join us again next time for more trending topics and useful vocabulary.

segments.speaker: Georgie
segments.text: Goodbye for now.

segments.speaker: Phil
